mechanism_fit: This realises R1 (M1 + M6, local oddness). The odd-looking but correct method is DurationFormatUtils.format. It is already present and unchanged. Its seconds-then-millis branch uses a sentinel-digit trick: it adds 1000, left-pads, then drops the leading digit with str.substring(1). The trick is valid for every normalised value 0..999, but it looks hacky. The gold is DurationFormatUtils.formatPeriod(long,long,String,boolean,TimeZone), and its fault is a quiet omission: the millisecond borrow loop (a normalisation step) is missing. The comment 'each initial estimate is adjusted in case it is under 0' stays, followed by the seconds/minutes/hours loops, so the body still reads as complete. Under the trigger, format receives seconds=35 and milliseconds=-500. Its trick then visibly mangles the millis field ('35.00' instead of '34.500'), so the failure looks local to the odd decoy, while the gold looks ordinary. A second, weaker competitor is lexx (it tokenises 'H:mm:ss.SSS'). Both decoys execute under the trigger (G6). The gold is also the entry point, so the gold is exposed and inspected; the screened question is whether the odd decoy is ranked above it.

Minimal repair: restore `while (milliseconds < 0) { milliseconds += 1000; seconds -= 1; }` before the seconds borrow loop.

ownership_reason: formatPeriod takes per-field differences of the two calendars. Under its comment 'each initial estimate is adjusted in case it is under 0', it normalises each negative field by borrowing from the next larger one: seconds, minutes and hours by while-loops, days and months further down. The millisecond difference is the only field left unadjusted. For the trigger (10:15:30.750 to 10:16:05.250 GMT, 34500 ms), formatPeriod therefore passes format() seconds=35 and milliseconds=-500. format() only renders the field values it is given. Its seconds-then-millis branch is correct for every normalised value 0..999. That is the range formatDuration always supplies, and the passing testFormatDurationHMS, testFormatDurationISO and testFormatPeriodISO pin that behaviour. The wrong seconds digit (35 instead of 34) is appended before the S token is processed, so no edit inside format()'s millisecond branch can repair the output. G9 confirms that three plausible one-line format() edits all leave the trigger failing. lexx tokenises the pattern correctly (testLexx passes). The minimal single-method repair restores the millisecond borrow in formatPeriod.
trigger: org.apache.commons.lang3.time.DurationFormatUtilsTest::testPeriodWithFractionalSeconds. It builds start = 2013-06-01 10:15:30.750 GMT and end = 2013-06-01 10:16:05.250 GMT with Calendar.getInstance(TimeZone.getTimeZone("GMT")) after cal.clear(). It then asserts assertEquals(34500L, end - start) and assertEquals("0:00:34.500", DurationFormatUtils.formatPeriod(start, end, "H:mm:ss.SSS", true, gmt)). The test is deterministic because the time zone is explicit and the dates are fixed. No imports were needed: Calendar and TimeZone are already imported.
